response.coreIdea: Dot products of longer random vectors spread out more, so attention divides them by the square root of the length to keep its weights soft.
response.title: Why attention divides by √d_k[[m1]]
response.dek: Longer vectors make the scores spread out.[[m2]] Dividing by √d_k keeps them in check.

sections.heading: Scores from dot products[[m1]]
paragraphs: A softmax turns scores into weights that add up to 1.[[m1]] Each weight is a share of the total.[[m2]]

sections.heading: Wider vectors, wilder scores
paragraphs: A dot product adds up d_k random terms, so its spread grows like √d_k.[[m1]] Drag d_k up and watch one key take all the weight.[[m9]]

sections.heading: The square-root law
paragraphs: [[vaswani]] divide every score by √d_k.[[Not an id!]] Drag x along the curve to read the spread for any width.

figures.title: Scaling keeps attention soft
figures.caption: Attention weights over eight keys for one random query.[[m2]] Drag d_k.
figures.alt: Bar chart of attention weights over eight keys at width 4, fairly even. As d_k grows without scaling, one bar takes almost all the weight; with scaling the bars stay spread.

figures.title: Spread grows like √d_k
figures.caption: The standard deviation of a dot product of two random d_k-wide vectors.
figures.alt: Line chart of score spread against key width from 1 to 512, rising like a square root: 2 at width 4, 8 at width 64, about 22.6 at width 512.

response.takeaway: The longer the vectors, the wider the scores spread, so attention divides every score by the square root of their length and its weights stay soft at any width.

notes.plain: Each weight is e raised to its score, as a share of the total over every key.
The spread of a sum of d_k independent terms, each with spread 1, is the square root of d_k.
